data.title: Tesla could transform the trucking business - and capitalize on high diesel prices
data.description:
By William Gavin

The EV maker aims to finally kick its long-awaited Semi truck into high gear - unlocking a potentially huge opportunity, according to Morgan Stanley

Tesla's all-electric Semi is the company's ticket to becoming a winner in autonomous trucking, analysts say.

Diesel prices have reached a new record, likely making everything from grocery shopping to commuting to work more expensive. But for Tesla, that price spike represents an opportunity.

Tesla (TSLA) is ramping up the Semi - a fully electric, heavy-duty semi truck that was introduced in late 2017 and began rolling off a high-volume production line in April. CEO Elon Musk has also said Tesla will aim to offer self-driving Tesla Semis by 2027.

Morgan Stanley analyst Andrew Percoco wrote on Friday that he long believed Tesla was a "potential wildcard in the competitive landscape" of autonomous trucks. Now, the company is becoming a "credible emerging competitor," he said.

Tesla plans to host an inauguration event on Sept. 24 for the Nevada facility that had previously outlined a production target of 50,000 Semis per year. The vehicle has attracted orders from several major companies including Walmart (WMT), PepsiCo (PEP) and Swedish electric-truck company Einride (ENRD), which aims to deploy 500 Semis.

Autonomous trucking could be a boon for the freight industry, thanks to a combination of lower labor costs and less fuel waste. Diesel costs are on the rise - reaching a new peak of $6 per gallon, on average, in the U.S. this week, according to AAA.

Percoco said that an autonomous fleet could be between six and eight times as profitable as a human-driven fleet. The "most important takeaway" for Tesla investors is what the company can make off its autonomous software, he noted. Tesla sells its Full Self-Driving advanced driver-assistance system to customers as a monthly subscription.

The analyst estimated that Tesla could generate between $12,000 and $18,000 per month for each vehicle, basing that figure off a subscription fee and an assumed amount of miles driven per month. By 2040, that could represent a $17 billion stream of software revenue, Percoco added, assuming that Tesla accounts for 13.5% of the market.

"Tesla Semi represents an underappreciated driver of earnings growth through 2040," he wrote.

Percoco, who is neutral on Tesla's stock, said his expectations for the Semi led him to raise the price target for his Tesla bull case to $840, from $820. His $400 base price target was left untouched.

Tesla's stock closed Friday up 0.5%, to trade at $365.44 a share.

There are a few caveats. In a separate note to clients, Morgan Stanley analyst Ravi Shanker warned that while autonomous trucking is "more real than ever," it's also still just a "promise" until commercial production ramps up in 2027. Most of the vehicles currently on the road, even those generating revenue, are still basically prototypes, he added.

Tesla has also put the Semi's self-driving software on the back burner as it focuses on the newly deployed Cybercab and its other vehicles. Musk told investors in July he doesn't want the Semi to "be a distraction" over the next several months.

Morgan Stanley also sees Aurora Innovation (AUR) and Kodiak AI (KDK) as potential autonomous-trucking winners. The firm expects Aurora to control 22.5% of the autonomous-vehicle market by 2040, while Kodiak would have an estimated 8.8% share.

Shanker raised his price target on Aurora's stock to $18 from $14, and initiated coverage on Kodiak's stock with a $9 price target. Morgan Stanley has a buy rating on Aurora's stock and the equivalent of a neutral rating on Kodiak's.

Aurora shares were up 1.6% on Friday to $6.43, while Kodiak shares declined 1.6% to $3.74.

-William Gavin

data.title: Salesforce's stock has been riding a wave of AI optimism. Here's what Wall Street wants to see next.
data.description:
By Hannah Pedone

Salesforce's Dreamforce conference next week could offer a glimpse of how its recently announced Claudeforce partnership with Anthropic will play out

Salesforce is expected to host its Dreamforce conference in San Francisco on Sept. 15-17.

Investors have been buying into the idea of Salesforce as a more formidable artificial-intelligence player, but that new narrative will be put to the test next week when the company hosts its annual Dreamforce conference in San Francisco.

The 23% surge in Salesforce's stock (CRM) the day after its earnings report last month wasn't just a referendum on the numbers, but also a vote of confidence in the company's AI strategy. Whether that momentum will continue remains up for debate, according to analysts.

UBS analyst Karl Keirstead wrote in a note that the investor focus at Dreamforce will be on the newly announced Claudeforce, a partnership that integrates Anthropic's Claude directly into the Salesforce platform.

The partnership combines the "reasoning capabilities of [Anthropic's] frontier models with the customer data, workflows, business logic and governance embedded in Salesforce," Keirstead explained.

"The centerpiece of the announcement was the introduction of a new plug-in that allows the frontier lab's users to access and act on Salesforce data directly through their platform," versus going through Salesforce's traditional user interface, or UI, he noted.

Keirstead said that while he views the partnership positively, it's too early to say how impactful it will be to the company's revenue growth for the 2028 fiscal year, which ends in January of that year.

See also: Building U.S. data centers is getting so expensive that AI companies are moving overseas

Needham analyst Scott Berg told MarketWatch that Claudeforce does mark a "strategy shift," but he still has questions over how customers might view the platform with the Claude configuration. Importantly, integrating Claude into Salesforce's platform causes Salesforce to cede control of its user interface layer in some ways; the company must give up control of where users access Salesforce data from, for instance.

"Will Salesforce giving up the UI for customers using Claude to access the Salesforce data negatively change how customers view the Salesforce platform?" Berg asked.

That's a concern for investors, because a negative change in the value of the platform could impact customers' willingness to pay for Salesforce's data and workflows. Another scenario would be that the partnership leads customers to unlock new functionalities and value from Salesforce's data. For now, it's "just too early to tell," Berg said.

Shares of Salesforce gained nearly 2% on Friday.

The Dreamforce conference kicks off on Sept. 15.

-Hannah Pedone

data.title: Oracle shook off fears about AI spending, but its stock still loses ground
data.description:
By Barbara Kollmeyer and Hannah Pedone

'Several of Oracle's bear cases were addressed head on' in the latest earnings report, according to an analyst

Oracle won praise from Wall Street analysts after its earnings report.

Analysts said Oracle helped dispel a string of investor concerns with its latest earnings report - but the stock's postearnings momentum didn't last long.

Shares of Oracle (ORCL) rose as much as 8.5% earlier on Friday, but later reversed course end the day down 1.7%.

While there's no doubt that Oracle is growing, a key issue for investors has been the level of spending required to drive that growth. But Piper Sandler analyst Billy Fitzsimmons noted after Thursday's report that the company opted to maintain its forecast for capital expenditures, or money put toward things like data centers and hardware. That's significant because there were fears that management would lift its spending outlook.

"Several of Oracle's bear cases were addressed head on," Fitzsimmons said in a note to clients.

Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler added that investor interest in Oracle's stock is high, and that those who don't currently own shares are looking "to understand the opportunity and gain confidence the bear concerns are wrong." To that end, the latest report boosted "clarity" around a positive investment case for Oracle's stock, he said.

"Oracle is not only executing well but also communicating better, with more details, clarity and increased confidence," Moerdler wrote. "The company is also diversifying its customer base while increasing RPO, which does not require meaningful additional cash requirements." RPO refers to remaining performance obligations, or the dollar value of contracted services that have yet to be delivered to customers or booked as revenue.

StoneX analyst Yi Fu Lee wrote in a Friday note that a big takeaway from Oracle's earnings was that Oracle Cloud Infrastructure saw 121% growth from the prior year. "Oracle continues signing large-scale AI-related contracts while emphasizing that customer demand still exceeds available supply," he wrote.

Lee said that the report shows that "enterprise AI continues moving beyond experimentation and into production deployment."

J.P. Morgan analysts pointed to an August quarter that they said eased key worries around data-center delays. Analysts led by Samik Chatterjee noted 850 megawatts of artificial-intelligence computing power were delivered in the quarter, three times what was seen in the May quarter. They also highlighted $30 billion-plus in new AI contracts.

"We got both better in-period execution and future-period bookings than anticipated. Check and check," observed Jackson Ader at KeyBanc Capital Markets.

Yet some analysts still had lingering concerns - especially surrounding gross margins, which measure the portion of revenue that a company retains after covering the costs of making its products. Morgan Stanley analyst Sanjit Singh said he wanted to see more stabilization of those margins as well as details on when new data centers will be up and running.

The next major event for Oracle is an analyst day expected to take place in October.

-Barbara Kollmeyer -Hannah Pedone

data.title: Why Dell and HPE were the S&P 500's top-performing stocks today
data.description:
By Britney Nguyen

Oracle's earnings provided an upbeat read for hardware suppliers, but the upcoming Fed decision on interest rates could dictate just how much they continue benefitting, an expert says

Dell's stock was up 12% on Friday.

Shares of server makers Dell Technologies and Hewlett Packard Enterprise led the S&P 500's gainers on Friday, as investors were reassured about data-center spending by Oracle's latest earnings report.

Oracle's (ORCL) 30% revenue growth and expanding backlog for its artificial-intelligence cloud services showed investors that AI spending "remains robust and can translate into revenue," according to Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management. That offered a boost to Dell (DELL) and HPE (HPE), which provide data-center hardware.

Mulberry also pointed to Dell's own recent earnings report, which showed its AI server business reaching $60.9 billion in orders and the company's backlog swelling to $95 billion.

Accelerating demand for traditional and AI servers, as well as storage and networking equipment, is benefitting both Dell and HPE, Mulberry said in emailed comments. He noted that Dell has greater exposure to large-scale orders for AI servers, while HPE has strength from its broad networking and enterprise infrastructure offerings.

HPE's stock gained 12.4% on Friday, setting an all-time closing high, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Dell's stock rose 12%, also booking a record close, the data showed.

RBC Capital Markets analyst David Paige initiated coverage of Dell's stock on Thursday with an outperform rating - writing in a note to clients that the company's "end-to-end portfolio across compute, PCs, storage and servers, along with its install base, best-in-class-supply chain and flexible consumption options," put it in a strong position to continue gaining share within the market for AI infrastructure.

Ryan Lee, senior vice president of product and strategy at Direxion, said strong results from cloud-services providers like Oracle often provide a tailwind for hardware makers that are supplying the data-center build-out.

Zooming out, however, Lee said the broader tech market is being driven by two things in the near term: oil prices (CL00) (BRN00) and next week's Federal Reserve policy meeting, at which the U.S. central bank could decide to raise interest rates.

If the Fed decides against raising rates, Lee said he expects many tech names to "be in very good shape." But if interest rates go up, as is the prevailing expectation, he said the reaction among AI-related stocks could vary.

"The reality is, when cost to borrow goes up, you're not going to see as favorable of a reaction for big-cap companies," Lee said, referring to companies with large market capitalizations. "Even the big dogs won't be able to escape a higher[-rate] environment."

Lee said investors will be watching the Fed's decision leading into November's midterm elections, as well as how oil prices unfold amid tensions between the U.S. and Iran, all of which will have implications for tech stocks.

In the long run, Lee said it will be worth watching how sticky massive AI spending continues to be given changes in the broader market and economic environment. "The answer the market has given so far is very sticky," he noted.

Therefore, Lee expects hardware suppliers like Dell and HPE to continue having an advantage in the short to medium term - but "how big of a beneficiary they are is going to be dictated by rates," he added.

-Britney Nguyen

data.title: I'm a single 58-year-old veteran in California with $1.5 million and a VA pension. Can I retire?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I expect to receive at least $9,000 per month before federal and California state taxes'

"Ultimately, I want to develop a retirement strategy that provides dependable income, tax efficiency, preservation of principal and inflation protection." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I am 58. I have $500,000 in stocks, ETFs, index and mutual funds; $330,000 in my 401(k)/Thrift Savings Plan; $295,000 in CDs; $117,000 in a deferred annuity; $180,000 in savings; $97,000 in Series I TreasuryDirect Savings Bonds; $10,000 in cash, for a total of $1.53 million, excluding the future value of my pensions, Social Security and VA benefits.

I am a GS-12, Step 3 federal employee earning $119,356 annually. I am also an O-5/LTC with 40 years in the U.S. Army Reserve and must retire from the USAR at age 60. I expect to receive at least $9,000 per month before federal and California state taxes from my retirement-related benefits. I will retain TRICARE and Veterans' Group Life Insurance (VGLI).

I also receive $4,000 a month in VA disability, and I am eligible for travel reimbursement to qualifying medical appointments. I plan to retire from federal employment at 62 with about 33 years of FERS creditable service after my military buyback/military service deposits and plan to retain Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) and FEGLI.

After federal retirement, I am considering working for another five years, potentially with CalPERS or the county, until 67. I currently estimate my Social Security benefit at $2,431 per month beginning at age 68, or the end of December 2035. I hope I can retire earlier without compromising my lifestyle or long-term security.

I am eligible for Veteran Readiness & Employment (VR&E) and intend to use it first to obtain additional education and skills. I also have 11 months and 20 days remaining under the Post-9/11 GI Bill. If eligible, I may attend community college and receive the applicable Masters of Health Administration (MHA).

I would prefer to retire in a location with no individual state income tax and ideally minimal sales and other taxes.

I am considering moving out of California in retirement, potentially to Anchorage, Alaska, or El Paso, Texas. I would prefer to retire in a location with no individual state income tax and ideally minimal sales and other taxes. I live in California, am single with no children or dependents, rent rather than own, have no mortgage, and am in the 24% federal tax bracket.

Am I financially ready to retire, and how much of my investment portfolio will I actually need? Does the traditional 4% rule apply to me, or could I safely withdraw significantly less because of my pensions, Social Security, and other income? How should I structure my $1.53 million portfolio to provide additional passive income while also offsetting inflation?

I'm looking for advice on tax-efficient retirement planning, including Roth conversions, withdrawal sequencing, required minimum distributions, and how to coordinate my taxable investments, TSP/401(k), CDs, annuity, Series I bonds, pensions, VA benefits, and Social Security. I would like to know whether I am holding too much in conservative assets.

I would also appreciate a comparison of California versus Alaska and Texas from an overall retirement perspective, including income taxes, sales taxes, cost of living, housing, and other significant expenses. Finally, I would like to understand whether marriage or having eligible dependents would materially increase my VA benefits.

Ultimately, I want to develop a retirement strategy that provides income, tax efficiency, preservation of principal and inflation protection. Rather than applying the 4% rule to my $1.53 million portfolio, I would like to understand how my various guaranteed and semi-guaranteed income sources change the amount I actually need to withdraw.

Hopeful Retiree

Don't miss: 'My main goal is to help people': I'm single, 74, with $10 million burning a hole in my pocket. What should I do?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

You have nearly $700,000, or 46% of your financial assets, in conservative vehicles that are, I assume, just about keeping up with inflation.

Dear Hopeful,

You are asking a lot of the right questions - except perhaps for one.

Wondering whether your $1.53 million will be enough to retire on is understandable. Based on the numbers and your projected retirement income, very likely yes. The more interesting - and, frankly, fortunate and unusual - question is whether you can spend your retirement years without ever needing to dip deeply into that honeypot at all.

Your assets, which will continue to rise over the next decade, military retirement, FERS, $4,000-a-month VA compensation, Social Security, TRICARE/FEHB, and potentially another five years of employment puts you in a stronger position than the average Joe. Assuming you have no debts, you are in solid shape with your monthly income.

You need a certified financial planner (CFP), the gold standard to run all of your different scenarios, taking into account your living expenses, and whether it's worth moving out of California in retirement to Texas or Alaska. Where you live is as much about the weather, culture, community, etc., as it is about taxes. Marry for love, not taxes.

You will have $9,000 a month in retirement and other income, $4,000 in VA compensation, and $2,431 a month in Social Security at 68, not to mention potentially five years of additional employment income that puts you at over $15,000 in monthly income, assuming the VA compensation and Social Security are not included in your $9,000 estimate.

Your $1.53 million portfolio is a nice cushion that you can draw from and/or with the help of your CFP, make strategic Roth conversions. After all, if you did withdraw 4% of that $1.53 million, you would get around $61,000 a year, or about $5,000 a month. Would that push you into a higher tax bracket and, if so, when? Your CFP can answer that.

Cautious vs. conservative

The big question will be timing your income from your various retirement accounts, investments and pensions, and when you have windows to make Roth conversions. Your CFP and/or a tax accountant should model your Roth conversions during those projected lower-income years, and whether it makes sense to take Social Security at 68, or wait until 70.

And now? I'd be more concerned about having too much of your money sitting in very conservative assets than about running out of money. You have roughly $700,000 - about 46% of your financial assets - in CDs, savings, Series I bonds, cash and your deferred annuity. That's a substantial amount of money in relatively conservative vehicles.

Does your monthly spending exceed income? Given your financial profile, and the fact that you are a single man with no children, I'm going to take a wild guess and suggest that you live a modest lifestyle. I say that because few people get to a position you are in at 58 without working hard, saving hard and thinking about retirement from a relatively young age.

Leaving California could be financially attractive because California's income-tax rates are not insignificant, particularly when you factor in your various pensions and investment income, all of which are considerable. In addition to state income tax, look at the cost of housing, insurance, property taxes, sales taxes, transportation, utilities and healthcare.

Ultimately, you are asking whether $1.53 million is enough to retire on. Based on the numbers, the more interesting question is whether you can spend your retirement years without ever tapping the lion's share of your investments, how you minimize your taxes (while being practical about your income) and what happens to your estate after you're gone.

Your investments look like the backup plan, rather than the main event.

data.title: Stellantis Talks With Canadian Workers Hit Impasse on Plan to Sell Ontario Factory, Union Says — Update
data.description:
By Paul Vieira 




  OTTAWA--Stellantis is in talks to sell its idled Toronto-area factory to a local defense firm, prompting the union representing over 9,000 of the automaker's Canadian employees to declare an impasse on talks toward a new labor deal. 



  The potential sale is the latest development involving the Stellantis factory in Brampton, Ontario, which hasn't operated since 2024 to undergo retooling. 



  Stellantis last year unveiled plans to shift the production of its next-generation Jeep Compass to Illinois from Brampton amid hefty Trump administration tariffs on foreign-made cars. The decision sparked the threat of a lawsuit from the Canadian government, which had provided Stellantis with hundreds of millions for work at the plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ontario. 



  Unifor, which represents auto-assembly workers, said Stellantis disclosed during talks on a new collective-bargaining agreement that the company had an interested buyer of the Brampton plant in a Canadian producer of smart-armored vehicles. 



  A Stellantis spokeswoman confirmed the interest from Canadian defense manufacturer Roshel, a maker of armored vehicles. Stellantis added that the two sides have signed a memorandum of understanding, which signals both companies' interest in pursuing a transaction. 



   "The persistence of the company's proposal to close and sell the Brampton plant has hindered the bargaining process," Unifor said, adding that talks have reached an impasse and are now paused. Unifor said the current labor deal expires on Aug. 20. 



  The Stellantis spokeswoman said Roshel represents the best option to restoring operations at its Brampton assembly plant, "preserving the site's strategic role in Canada's advanced manufacturing sector and helping to avoid a prolonged period of inactivity." She had no further comment, citing collective-bargaining talks with Unifor. 



  Representatives for Roshel didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. In interviews with Canadian media this summer, the company's chief executive, Roman Shimonov, said he was interested in the idle Brampton plant as the company required more factory space to meet demand. 



  "We know that many automotive companies pulled out from Canada, and that's exactly where defence can substitute and bring thousands of employees back, including in Brampton," Shimonov said at the time. 



  A spokeswoman for Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. 



  Government officials have been in talks about the future of the Brampton plant. Joly has threatened to launch a lawsuit against Stellantis, for failing to follow through with the Jeep Compass production, and vowed to recover the millions of dollars that governments provided to the car maker. 



  Trade relations between the U.S. and Canada have deteriorated in the past three weeks after talks unexpectedly collapsed toward a new trade pact, with both sides blaming the other for raising last-minute demands. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the negotiations with the U.S. revealed that the Trump administration wanted "to destroy our major industries, including our auto industry."

Saudi Arabia Shuts Down Pipeline That Was a Crucial Hormuz Bypass

data.title: ANV Strengthens US Transactional Risk Platform
data.description:
ANV Strengthens US Transactional Risk Platform

ANV Group Holdings Ltd. (“ANV” or “the Company”), a global insurance intermediary platform, today announced the appointment of Sarthak Sharma to lead US Transactional Risk within ANV, and confirmed the departure of Colin Addy and Greg Conroy.

Sharma brings nearly a decade of insurance and legal experience spanning transactional risk, underwriting, and mergers and acquisitions. In his new role, he will lead ANV’s US Transactional Risk team, with a focus on growing the business, strengthening broker relationships and delivering specialized insurance solutions for complex M&A transactions.

“Sarthak brings deep transactional risk expertise, strong underwriting and legal experience, and a proven ability to build trusted relationships across the M&A market,” said Aaron Basilius, Executive Vice President, Head of US MGAs at ANV. “His leadership will be instrumental as we continue to grow ANV’s US Transactional Risk platform.”

Prior to joining ANV, Sharma served as Senior Vice President & Counsel, Mergers & Acquisitions at Ryan Transactional Risk, where he specialized in representations and warranties insurance and worked closely with brokers, strategic buyers and private equity firms on complex M&A transactions.

“I’m excited to join ANV and lead its US Transactional Risk business,” said Sharma. “There is a strong opportunity to create a differentiated offering centered on underwriting expertise, broker relationships, and I look forward to building something meaningful alongside the broader ANV team.”

ANV confirmed that Colin Addy and Greg Conroy have left the Company to pursue other opportunities. “We thank Colin and Greg for their dedicated service and contributions to building and growing our US Transaction Risk business,” said Aaron Basilius. “During their tenure, Colin and Greg played an important role in the Company’s development and helped establish a strong foundation for success. We are grateful for their leadership, commitment, efforts on behalf of the Company and its clients. We wish them continued success moving forward."

About ANV Group Holding Ltd.

ANV Group Holdings Ltd. (“ANV”) is an independent, global insurance intermediary platform operating across the United States, the United Kingdom and Europe. The company brings together a portfolio of established specialist MGAs, providing a diversified range insurance products. For more information about ANV, visit http://www.anvinsurance.com.
